strengths: Addresses a clinically important problem: reducing annotation burden in medical imaging by using a reference image to guide anatomical identification, localization, and segmentation.

Proposes a unified framework that connects VLM spatial reasoning with SAM2 memory-based segmentation, and evaluates it on multiple modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound) and tasks (VQA, bbox prediction, segmentation).
Shows substantial quantitative improvements over several baselines, including strong reported OOD generalization on LERA and CAMUS, which is important for medical deployment.
Uses a reasonable two-stage training recipe (SFT followed by GRPO-based RL) and includes useful components such as global matching via optimal transport and SAM2 memory integration.
Provides qualitative examples, an initialization ablation, hyperparameters, and appendix dataset descriptions, giving some support for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the paper mainly integrates existing components (VLM, SAM2, LoRA, GRPO, optimal transport) rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithm; the 'first to explore' claim is broad and not fully substantiated.

Experimental rigor is limited by missing controls: there is no no-reference ablation to verify that the reference image itself is driving the claimed relative spatial reasoning, rather than target-image label fitting.

Patient-level data splits for RAOS and Arcade are not clearly described; if target slices or reference banks overlap with training patients, the reported ID results are not trustworthy. The paper also reports no seeds, error bars, or statistical significance tests.

Baseline comparisons are questionable: Table 1 compares a fine-tuned model against zero-shot MedFlamingo/MedVLM-R1, which is not apples-to-apples; segmentation baselines (SAM2-Memory, SAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT) may be under-trained or poorly tuned, making the very large reported gaps less convincing.

Several important ablations are missing: no comparison to other VLM grounding methods (e.g., LISA, Grounding DINO), no atlas/registration or nnU-Net-style baseline, no ablation on global matching, memory design, or reference selection, and no analysis of failure cases beyond qualitative examples.

There are multiple serious citation errors: GLIP is cited as Balibar & Walsh (2006), OWL-ViT as Alhadidi et al. (2024), SEEM as Nasser & Chen (2007), and Grounding DINO/Mask2Former citations appear incorrect. This reflects poor attribution and carelessness.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: inconsistent training-set size (650k vs. 450k), no code release, no training time or inference cost, and unclear how reference images are selected at test time for each dataset.
The claim of 'seamless' integration overstates the engineering effort, as the method requires training an MLP projection and fine-tuning the SAM2 decoder, plus a two-stage SFT/RL pipeline.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations or societal-impact discussion, including concerns about requiring annotated reference images, cross-population bias, clinical safety, and computational cost.

The reported CoT reasoning analysis is qualitative and cherry-picked in Figure A1; there is no systematic evaluation showing that the model actually performs relative spatial reasoning rather than learning dataset-specific shortcuts.

strengths: Tackles a practically important problem—label-efficient anatomical understanding—by coupling reference-based reasoning with segmentation, which is well motivated for medical imaging where annotated data is scarce.

The architecture combining a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), a LISA-style <Seg> token with an MLP regressor, an optimal-transport global matching step, and SAM2's memory bank is coherent and technically sensible as an integration of existing parts.

Evaluation spans multiple modalities (CT, X-ray angiography, skeletal X-ray, ultrasound) and includes both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, which is a reasonable effort at demonstrating generalization.
The manuscript is generally well written and the task formulations (VQA, bbox, segmentation) are described clearly with explicit equations.
Reported OOD improvements over the SAM2 memory baseline are large and, if reproducible, could be practically useful for reference-driven medical segmentation.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the framework is essentially an assembly of existing components—LISA's <Seg> token + MLP (Lai et al., 2024), SAM2's memory attention (Ravi et al., 2024), DINOv2 retrieval, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024)—applied to medical reference images. No new method, supervision scheme, or theoretical insight is introduced beyond task-specific engineering.

Baselines are weak and unrepresentative of the state of the art. The SAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT baseline (Dice ≈ 0.19) is far below what a reasonable prompt- or memory-based segmentation baseline should achieve; without stronger baselines (e.g., MedSAM with VLM-predicted boxes/points, nnU-Net, atlas-registration pipelines, retrieval-augmented few-shot segmentation such as Zhao et al., 2025, or SAMed), the substantial segmentation gains in Table 3 are hard to interpret.

Key relevant families of prior work are missing from quantitative comparison: classical atlas/registration-based label propagation (the natural reference-based baseline in medical imaging) and existing retrieval-based few-shot segmentation methods. nnU-Net is only mentioned qualitatively, so the paper's claim to strong granular segmentation is under-supported.

The 'reference-guided relational reasoning' claim is weakly evidenced. The reasoning analysis rests on a single anecdotal CoT example (Fig. A1) rather than a systematic, quantitative study of reasoning traces, leaving the central narrative about VLM spatial reasoning only loosely supported.

Reporting and evaluation protocol are unclear: Tables 2 and 4 report 'best score' labeling accuracy without defining what 'best' means (best over checkpoints? best over classes?), and no error bars, seeds, or variance are provided, making the large OOD deltas difficult to trust.

Data separation and potential leakage are not addressed. Training corpora are built by 'cross-patient slice matching' within RAOS/Arcade, but it is unclear whether test patients, slices, or templates are strictly held out, and whether the OOD reference templates are drawn from the target-domain test distribution—either would change the difficulty of the task substantially.

Overstated claims: the 'first to explore VLMs for reference-based identification/localization/segmentation' claim is strong and not carefully substantiated against reference-based segmentation literature; the broader contribution is a task-specific combination rather than a mechanistic discovery.

Ablations are limited: only VLM initialization is ablated (vanilla/SFT/RL). No ablation on the optimal-transport global matching, the memory attention fusion, the MLP projection, or the reward components, so it is unclear which pieces drive the reported gains.

OOD scope is narrow: only two OOD datasets (LERA, CAMUS) support the strong generalization claims, and the LERA jump (33.95% → 61.87%) is not analyzed; without stronger baselines and per-class breakdowns, it is unclear whether improvements stem from reasoning, template retrieval, or the memory mechanism.

AN 'Applied/Systems' framing would be more apt than a methodological one, but even under that framing the system-level novelty is thin and the empirical comparison is insufficient to support the framing of the paper as a new reference-based understanding paradigm.

strengths: Proposes a clinically motivated reference-based anatomical understanding task for medical imaging and demonstrates it across VQA, bounding-box, and segmentation outputs.

Effectively combines VLM fine-tuning/GRPO, optimal-transport global matching, and SAM2 memory for pixel-level segmentation; the experimental results on ID/OOD datasets show strong gains over VLM and SAM2/MedSAM2 baselines.
Ablations support the key claims: RL improves over SFT, shuffled references degrade performance, and VLM-guided SAM2 segmentation substantially outperforms memory-only baselines.
Reproducibility details are largely provided (datasets, hyperparameters, compute setup, LLM usage), and the paper includes qualitative examples plus failure-case and reference-quality analyses.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is primarily integrative: reference-based VLM reasoning, GRPO, SAM2 memory, and optimal transport are existing components, so the algorithmic contribution is more engineering-oriented than conceptually new.

The bounding-box stage is evaluated mainly by labeling accuracy after global matching, not by standard localization metrics such as box IoU or AP, so the quality of the predicted boxes is not fully established.

Segmentation comparisons lack standard supervised or registration/atlas-based anatomical segmentation baselines, and it is not fully clear that the SAM2/MedSAM2 baselines represent the strongest alternatives.

The framework assumes an annotated reference image at inference time, which weakens the stated data-efficiency advantage; reference retrieval/selection and its impact on OOD performance are not fully explored in the main paper.

Some claims, such as being the first to explore VLM-based reference anatomical understanding, are stronger than the presented related-work discussion fully supports, and prior reference/few-shot medical segmentation work could be more directly addressed.
